Only the meaning of discourse is genuinely human and therefore historical and dialectical.
Meaningful discourse is always dialectical, and dialectic is realized both in meaningful discourse and in the “ideal” world that discourse creates.
But this ideal world is not the only embodiment of dialectic.
The historical world is larger than the “ideal” world.
It rests on a “real” human world, which is no longer the world of discourse but the world of work and struggle.
This real world provides the actual foundation for the “ideological superstructure” of the “ideal” world of discourse and culture in general.
Without this real historical world, the ideal historical world could not exist.
Conversely, this real world is human, historical, and dialectical only because it supports that ideological superstructure.
Human beings speak because they work and struggle.
Yet they work and struggle as human beings, rather than as animals, precisely because they do not merely work and struggle. They also speak about their work and their struggle.
And they can speak about them only because they work and struggle differently from animals.
Here again we encounter the elusive “something” mentioned earlier—the very thing that realizes what we call dialectic.
There is no need to repeat what has already been said.
We need only note that the presence of this “something other” transforms a collection of “human” individuals into genuinely human societies and States—that is, historical or dialectical ones.
It likewise transforms the changes those individuals make to the natural world into genuinely human, and therefore historical or dialectical, technology.
Since the real historical world is based on work, we can call it the technical or “economic” world.
But since it is also based on struggle, we can call it the “political” world—or the “historical” world in the narrower sense.
It is obvious that there is no politics or technology without human beings. But we must add that there are no human beings without technology and politics either.
Like meaningful discourse and “culture” in general, technology and politics are forms of interaction with the natural world.
The “technical” human being—the person who works—and the “political” human being—the person who struggles—are therefore every bit as dialectical as the “cultural” human being—the person who speaks.
And the historical world of technology and politics is just as dialectical as the ideal historical world of meaningful discourse.

Conversely, dialectic is realized not only in human discourse and in the “ideal” world that discourse constructs. It is also realized in the real historical world of politics and technology created through human work and struggle.
Dialectic, then, is nothing other than the human being creating the historical world, both ideal and real.
Or, which comes to the same thing, dialectic is nothing other than the historical world created by human beings—or, more precisely, the historical world that human beings are continually creating.
It is therefore the process through which human beings create the historical world—and create themselves only in and through that process of creating the world.
But even this process does not completely exhaust dialectic.
In a certain sense, the natural world as a whole also realizes dialectic insofar as it includes human beings and therefore enters into interaction with them.
The historical—that is, human and dialectical—world in the broad sense is not only created by human beings.
To turn a natural thing into a “cultural” or “historical,” and therefore dialectical, thing, human beings do not necessarily have to alter it physically.
It is enough for them to enter into a real relation with it, provided that what enters into that relation is genuinely human and not merely the human animal body.
The fact that human beings breathe air does not make air “historical.” Animals breathe it too.

But the rock on which the Acropolis of Athens stands is just as “historical” as the building erected on it. It realizes dialectic just as much—not insofar as it is a natural rock, but insofar as it functions, so to speak, as the “foundation” of the Parthenon.
The sea is, in itself, a purely natural “thing.”
By itself it is not dialectical in any way, and nothing that happens within it, such as the cycle of the tides, has anything to do with dialectic.
Nor does the sea become dialectical merely because people decide to swim in it, since animals swim too.
But human beings do not merely splash around in the sea. They also work on and around it, and they struggle over it.
Since human work and struggle are dialectical, “working at sea” and “fighting over the sea” are dialectical too.
And because the “sea” enters into this dialectical phenomenon, the sea itself thereby becomes dialectical.
But work at sea, although it is specifically work at sea rather than somewhere else, is dialectical not because it takes place at sea, but because it is work at sea.
The same applies to struggle over the sea.
The Mediterranean, for example, was not the same thing for the Greeks of Pericles’ time as it was for the Italians of the Renaissance or for the British of our own time.
In this sense, the Mediterranean is historical and therefore dialectical. It changes according to the law of dialectical triads.
But by itself, outside its relation to human beings, it does not change in this way at all. It remains eternally what it is.
Taken by itself, therefore, it has nothing to do with dialectic.
More generally, the natural world is dialectical only insofar as it enters into interaction with what is human in human beings and thereby becomes part of the historical world.
But this interaction does not necessarily change the natural side of the world physically, as work does when it builds roads, digs canals, plants forests, clears woodland, and so on.
The natural world becomes historical—and therefore dialectical—as soon as it becomes the subject of human discourse or, more generally, an object of specifically human experience or consciousness.
A “birch tree,” for example, is not itself dialectical. But the “sensory perception of the birch tree” is dialectical, just as the science of the natural world in general is dialectical.
First, it is the human being as such, insofar as a human being differs from an animal.
Second, it is the ideal and real historical world—the technical and political world—created by human beings.
Third, it is the natural world, not taken in itself but taken as a phenomenon: insofar as it “appears” to a human being or to human consciousness through human knowledge.
The natural world in itself, by contrast, has nothing to do with dialectic.

The claim that the dialectical coincides with the human or historical—and conversely, that the human or historical coincides with the dialectical—can be fully demonstrated only by the System of Philosophy as a whole.
Here, then, I will make only two general remarks that may serve as arguments for my claim that only the human world is dialectical, while the natural world is not.
If we are willing to tolerate an anachronism, we can say that the Greeks discovered the non-dialectical character of the natural world.

They understood that nature is, so to speak, an eternal “thesis” to which it is pointless—and indeed impossible—to oppose an antithesis, unless we choose to regard non-being or nothingness as such an antithesis.
Nature remains eternally unchanged, everywhere and always identical with itself.
And this discovery enabled the Greeks to lay the foundations of genuine science of the natural world—the same structure we are still building today.
All natural science rests on the principle that nature is not historical and does not depend on time.
An oxygen atom was the same before human beings appeared as it was in Pushkin’s time and as it is today, and it will remain the same after humanity has disappeared.
It is only for this reason that exact and unchanging knowledge of it is possible.
And what is true of the atom is equally true of the “laws of nature” in general.
They are all “eternal” and unchanging through time.

This is the basis of the difference between natural science and the science of human beings. We can, for example, predict a solar eclipse a thousand years from now with complete accuracy—a mere trifle on the cosmic scale—because the solar system is not dialectical. It always remains what it is. But because human beings are dialectical, it is completely impossible for us to predict how or when even an event as close and historically important as the war between England and Germany will end.

This also explains the difference between technology and politics, and between the “technical” and “political” testing of knowledge. The laws that made it possible to build the Eiffel Tower in Paris are not dialectical. Its ability to remain standing is therefore enough to confirm their truth. We know that if the tower could have been built five thousand years ago, it would not have collapsed; and if another were built five thousand years from now, that one would not collapse either. By contrast, a policy that tried to apply to modern Italy the dialectical laws that once made the Roman Empire possible—for example, the laws governing slavery—would soon lead to disaster.

In short, the existence of natural science and technology would be completely incomprehensible if we assumed that nature obeyed the Hegelian or Marxist laws of dialectic. Since the existence of science and technology is beyond doubt, it is natural to suppose that the natural world does not in fact obey these laws. Otherwise, we would have to treat the very existence of science and technology as an inexplicable “miracle.”

We could reach the same conclusion by looking only at the human world. Its dialectical existence would itself become a “miracle” unless we assumed that it exists within something non-dialectical—in other words, within nature. If the world as a whole changed dialectically or historically, history itself would become impossible, because we would no longer be able to understand past historical periods. A period is historical only insofar as it somehow preserves the “memory” of an earlier period—which means that it can understand it.

To say that human beings are dialectical, or historical, is to say that they change in an essential way over time. A Greek living in the age of Pericles thinks and feels differently from us. So when he uses the Greek words for “virtue,” “love,” “beauty,” and so on, he does not mean exactly what we mean when we use those same words—say, in Russian.
Yet we know this Greek only through what he said or wrote.

Suppose the entire Greek language consisted only of words referring to human beings. How could we translate it—that is, understand it? Even if we know that the word philia means love, we still have to ask: what kind of love? What did the Greeks mean by it? Greek love—even love for a woman—is not the same as ours. So we would be ignorant not only of the word but also of the thing it refers to, because we can reach that thing only through the word. We would have, so to speak, an equation with two unknowns and no way to solve it. The Greeks might try to explain what their kind of love was, but if all their words were of this kind, we would never understand the explanation.
And yet in reality we understand them perfectly well—or at least well enough for their speech to affect our own perceptions and thereby make those perceptions historical or dialectical.

Because the overwhelming majority of Greek words do not refer to human beings but to nature. And if nature is not dialectical, then it is the same today as it was in the time of the Greeks. So if we learn that hyppos, for example, means “horse,” we immediately know what is being referred to. The word does not mean a specifically “Greek” horse. It means the horse in general, which is no different from our own.

In other words, we can immediately understand a discourse only because it also refers to a natural world that is no different from ours. And experience shows that, in the end, every discourse about human beings can be reduced to generally understandable words referring to this natural world that is common to everyone.
That is why—and the only reason why—such discourse can be understood by everyone, which is to say translated into every language.

Dialectical or historical existence itself, then, necessarily depends on this ability to understand the past. And this is possible only because dialectical existence is inseparably connected with non-dialectical existence. Everything therefore leads us to suppose that this non-dialectical existence is precisely the existence of the natural world.

These brief remarks may of course fail to convince the reader. But for the moment that does not matter very much. We need to accept the non-dialectical character of nature if we are to construct a true Ontology and Cosmology. For Phenomenology, however, it makes no difference at all. As we know, Phenomenology is first and foremost an anthropology: a discourse about human beings.

No Hegelian and no Marxist doubts that human beings are dialectical. If, in their view, all existence is dialectical, then human existence is obviously dialectical all the more so. And since Phenomenology studies not the natural world in itself but the world as a phenomenon—that is, as it “appears” to human beings—non-dialectical existence does not really belong to its subject matter.
From my point of view, then, everything in Phenomenology must be entirely dialectical.

Phenomenology deals with the dialectic that takes place in human beings and in the historical world they build, describing that world as an “appearance” or “phenomenon.” Hegel and Marx clearly assume that, alongside this dialectic, there is also some other, “natural” dialectic. But the important point is that they also recognize the existence of this specifically human dialectic.
What, then, does this dialectic consist in?

Hegel calls negativity (Negativität) the root, the nerve, or, better, the driving force of dialectic. He contrasts this negativity, which lies at the foundation of every dialectical form of existence, with identity (Identität), which by itself defines every form of non-dialectical existence.

In other words, non-dialectical existence—the kind of existence that, before Hegel, was regarded as the only possible kind of existence at all, and which we still contrast with dialectical existence by calling it “natural”—is defined by the fact that it is eternally unchanging. It always remains identical with itself, always equal to itself, and never passes beyond the limits assigned to it once and for all.

Of course, these definitions cannot be applied literally to every form of non-dialectical existence, or to every natural “thing.” But there are certain phenomena in the natural world to which they can be applied literally: the ultimate constituents of that world, the parts that supposedly cannot be broken down any further. For the Greeks these were the “elements” or “atoms”; for contemporary physics they are “electrons,” “protons,” and so on.

For contemporary physics, for example, electrons exist eternally. They neither come into being nor disappear. Their qualities, fixed once and for all from all “eternity,” never change anywhere or in any respect. So once you know one electron, you know them all; and if you know one now, you know what an electron is at any time.

It is true that Christian scientists of earlier centuries—Descartes and Newton, for example—believed in the doctrine of the “creation of the world” and accepted that the world might one day disappear. But this made little difference in principle. For them, the atom or its equivalent was created “out of nothing” and instantly endowed, so to speak, with all its qualities. Those qualities would then remain unchanged until the atom finally “fell back into non-being.”

The same can be said of the natural world as a whole. Scientists either assumed that it was “created” and would “disappear” in a single instant, or they regarded it as eternal—as something that had always existed and would never perish.
But the concept of “identity” cannot be applied literally even to an eternal world, because although such a world is eternal, it is not completely unchanging. It is not totally identical with itself.

Classical “corpuscular” physics assumed that only the atoms and their total number remained “eternally unchanged,” while their combinations constantly changed. Contemporary physics, by contrast, holds that only the total quantity of “matter” and “energy”—or perhaps energy alone—remains eternally unchanged, while the forms taken by matter and energy change.

This leads to a distinction of enormous importance, first recognized by the Greeks and now basic to all scientific thought: the distinction between essential qualities or characteristics—also called “primary,” “necessary,” and so on—and inessential qualities or characteristics—“secondary,” “contingent,” and so on.

For classical physics, for example, the “essential” characteristics were those belonging to atoms as such. The qualities produced by the various combinations of these atoms were regarded as “inessential,” “secondary,” “subjective,” and so on.
For contemporary physics, by contrast, only what belongs to “matter” itself and to “energy” is essential. Everything else is inessential.

In other words, we could know exhaustively what the world as a whole is simply by knowing these “essential” qualities. They would tell us what the world “really” or “essentially” is, whereas the “inessential” qualities would show only how the world appears to us.

This is why scientific knowledge—universally necessary, final, and unchanging knowledge, or knowledge that is genuinely true in the strongest sense—is possible only with respect to “essential” qualities. Of the “inessential” qualities we can have only more or less plausible “opinions,” which must continually be corrected and revised.

And this is clearly because essential qualities are eternal and unchanging: they remain “identical,” always equal to themselves. We can say that every eternally unchanging or identical quality is essential, and every essential quality is identical.
Natural science studies all such qualities and only such qualities. In short, it studies the world insofar as the world is “identical”—that is, eternally unchanging.

What is true of the world as a whole is also true of every natural “thing” within it. Science deals with things only insofar as they remain eternally equal to themselves and possess once and for all the unchanging qualities in question.

A chemist, for example, studies gold. But “pure” gold appears in many forms: nuggets, bars, rings, earrings, and so on. None of this matters very much to the chemist. What he wants are gold’s “essential” qualities—the qualities that remain unchanged whatever form the gold takes.
